# 1. Introduction and Problem Statement / Motivation

## 1.1 Project Background and Motivation

Football results are difficult to predict. A stronger team may be more likely to win, but injuries, tactics, home advantage and random events during a match can still change the result. Even so, pre-match data may contain useful patterns. This project investigates whether those patterns can be used to classify a match as a **home win**, **draw**, or **away win** across Europe's top five domestic leagues.

## 1.2 Research Question

The main research question is: **To what extent can pre-match team and match characteristics classify football match outcomes in Europe's top five domestic leagues as a home win, draw, or away win?** We compare five classification methods using the same engineered features and the same chronological split. This makes the comparison fair and ensures that differences in performance come from the models rather than different versions of the data. Accuracy alone is not enough here because a model can score reasonably well by predicting home wins too often. Draws are less common and are especially easy to miss, so Macro-F1 is used as the main selection metric. Accuracy, balanced accuracy, class-level precision, recall and F1, together with confusion matrices, provide additional detail.


## 1.3 Data Source and Study Scope

The dataset contains 25,241 matches from the top divisions of England, Spain, Italy, France and Germany, covering the 2012/13 to 2025/26 seasons. The response variable is `result`, classified as `home_win`, `draw` or `away_win`. Because home wins are the largest class and draws the smallest, model performance is assessed across all three outcomes rather than by accuracy alone.

The predictors use only information available before kick-off, including differences in league position, season points per game, recent form, recent goal difference, venue form, head-to-head history and rest days, together with league and season progress. Post-match goals, aggregate scores and supplied club positions were excluded to prevent leakage, while attendance, referee, formation, manager and snapshot club attributes were omitted because they were unavailable before kick-off, inconsistently recorded or historically inaccurate.

The analysis uses a chronological split: matches from 2012/13 to 2022/23 form the training set, while 2023/24 to 2025/26 form the untouched Final Test. Five expanding-window folds within the training period support tuning and model selection, with each validation season predicted using only earlier seasons. This design reflects the practical task of forecasting future matches and prevents future information from entering model development.

# 2. Exploratory Data Analysis

## 2.1 Outcome Distribution

```{r}
#| label: outcome-distribution
model_data <- readRDS("data/model_data.rds")
outcome_table <- as.data.frame(table(model_data$result))
names(outcome_table) <- c("Outcome", "Matches")
outcome_table$Percentage <- sprintf(
  "%.1f%%", 100 * outcome_table$Matches / sum(outcome_table$Matches)
)
knitr::kable(outcome_table, caption = "Match outcomes in the modelling dataset")
```

## 2.2 Data Quality and Missing Values

```{r}
#| label: fig-missingness
#| fig-cap: "Missing values among the engineered pre-match features."
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)

feat_cols <- c("table_pos_diff", "points_per_game_diff", "form_points_diff",
               "recent_goal_diff", "venue_form_diff", "h2h_diff", "rest_days_diff")
miss <- sapply(model_data[feat_cols], function(x) sum(is.na(x)))
miss_dt <- data.table(feature = names(miss), share = miss / nrow(model_data))
miss_dt <- miss_dt[share > 0]

ggplot(miss_dt, aes(reorder(feature, share), share)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share missing") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Missingness is modest and concentrated in features that depend on match history: `h2h_diff` is missing for 10.0% of matches (a club's first meeting) and `venue_form_diff` for 5.7%; the rest are under 3%. No feature exceeds 10% missing, so every model uses training-fold median imputation plus a missingness indicator rather than dropping rows, keeping the full 25,241-match sample.

## 2.3 Predictor Relationships and Key Patterns

```{r}
#| label: fig-corr-eda
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Correlation between the seven engineered differential features."
diff_feats <- c("table_pos_diff", "points_per_game_diff", "form_points_diff",
                "recent_goal_diff", "venue_form_diff", "h2h_diff", "rest_days_diff")
cor_mat <- cor(model_data[diff_feats], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor_long <- as.data.table(as.table(cor_mat))
setnames(cor_long, c("Var1", "Var2", "r"))

ggplot(cor_long, aes(Var1, Var2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r)), size = 2.8) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2171b5", mid = "white", high = "#cb181d",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "r")
```

Several features overlap strongly: `table_pos_diff` and `points_per_game_diff` correlate at r = 0.90, and `form_points_diff` and `recent_goal_diff` at r = 0.88 — each pair captures essentially the same signal measured two ways. LDA inverts a covariance matrix across predictors, so near-duplicate features destabilise its fitted coefficients; the weaker feature in each pair is dropped before fitting LDA (Section 3.4.2). Tree-based models split on one variable at a time and keep all nine features.

## 2.4 Implications for Modelling

Three EDA findings shaped the LDA model design below: the imbalanced outcome (home win 44.4%, draw 25.1%) motivates Macro-F1 as the primary metric; modest, history-dependent missingness (≤10%) is handled with training-fold median imputation and a missingness indicator rather than dropping rows; and the strong collinearity between several differential features motivates dropping the redundant member of each pair before fitting LDA, which depends on inverting a stable covariance matrix.

## 3.4 Classification Models

### 3.4.1 Multinomial Logistic Regression

Multinomial logistic regression (MLR) was fitted to predict **home win**, **draw**, or **away win**. The context-only baseline used `competition_id` and `season_progress`; the refined candidates added pre-match league position, season points per game, recent form, recent goal difference, venue form, head-to-head history and rest-day differences. Variables known only after kick-off were excluded.

All models used the shared chronological design: seasons through 2022/23 formed the training period and 2023/24–2025/26 formed the untouched Final Test. Five expanding-window folds within training were used for model selection. In every fold, missing-value medians, missingness indicators and standardisation parameters were estimated from the training portion only and then applied unchanged to its validation season. `competition_id` was retained as a factor.

```{r}
#| label: mlr-load-results
library(data.table)
library(knitr)

# The complete fitting and tuning pipeline is kept in R/member1_mlr.R.
# If the saved result is absent, this rebuilds it from the shared data,
# expanding-window folds and evaluate_model() scoring function.
if (!file.exists("outputs/member1_mlr_results.rds")) {
  source("R/member1_mlr.R")
}
mlr <- readRDS("outputs/member1_mlr_results.rds")
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
```

**Hyperparameter Tuning**

Several refined specifications were compared because the strength and form measures were correlated. Each feature set was tested with coefficient-decay values of 0, 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1 and 1. The ordinary largest-probability decision rule almost never predicted a draw, so draw and away-win probability weights were also tuned using validation predictions only. Mean validation Macro-F1 determined the final specification.

```{r}
#| label: mlr-tuning
cv <- as.data.table(mlr$cv_table)
best_by_set <- cv[order(-cv_macro_f1), .SD[1], by = feature_set]
tuning_table <- best_by_set[, .(
  `Feature set` = feature_set,
  Decay = decay,
  `Plain Macro-F1` = f3(cv_macro_f1_plain),
  `Draw weight` = w_draw,
  `Away weight` = w_away,
  `Weighted Macro-F1` = f3(cv_macro_f1)
)]
kable(tuning_table,
      caption = "Best validation result for each MLR feature set")
```

The selected model excluded `venue_form_diff`, used decay 0.1, and applied home/draw/away decision weights of 1.0/2.0/1.4. It achieved mean validation Macro-F1 of 0.462. The exclusion of venue form was based on future-season validation performance rather than correlation alone.

**Final Test Results and Interpretation**

```{r}
#| label: mlr-test-results
comparison <- as.data.table(mlr$comparison)
test_table <- comparison[, .(
  Model = stage,
  Accuracy = f3(accuracy),
  `Balanced Accuracy` = f3(balanced_accuracy),
  `Macro-F1` = f3(macro_f1),
  `Recall: Home` = f3(recall_home_win),
  `Recall: Draw` = f3(recall_draw),
  `Recall: Away` = f3(recall_away_win)
)]
kable(test_table, caption = "Multinomial logistic regression results on the Final Test")
```

```{r}
#| label: mlr-per-class-results
per_class <- as.data.table(mlr$test_metrics$per_class)
per_class_table <- per_class[, .(
  Class = c("Home win", "Draw", "Away win"),
  Precision = f3(precision),
  Recall = f3(recall),
  F1 = f3(f1)
)]
kable(per_class_table,
      caption = "Class-specific performance of the final multinomial logistic regression")
```

The ordinary refined MLR reached accuracy 0.510 but almost never predicted draws, resulting in Macro-F1 of 0.380. The validation-tuned decision rule reduced accuracy to 0.468 but increased draw recall to 0.375 and achieved test Macro-F1 of 0.457. Its class F1 scores were 0.558 for home wins, 0.326 for draws and 0.487 for away wins. Under the pre-specified primary metric, the weighted version was therefore selected because it provided more balanced performance across the three outcomes.

```{r}
#| label: mlr-confusion-matrix
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Final refined MLR confusion matrix. Percentages show recall within each true outcome."
class_labels <- c(home_win = "Home win", draw = "Draw", away_win = "Away win")
cm_data <- as.data.table(as.data.frame(mlr$test_metrics$confusion))
cm_data[, Share := Freq / sum(Freq), by = Truth]
cm_data[, Truth := factor(class_labels[as.character(Truth)], levels = class_labels)]
cm_data[, Predicted := factor(class_labels[as.character(Predicted)],
                              levels = rev(class_labels))]

ggplot(cm_data, aes(Truth, Predicted, fill = Share)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%d\n(%.0f%%)", Freq, 100 * Share)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f7fbff", high = "#2166ac", guide = "none") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  labs(x = "True result", y = "Predicted result")
```

The MLR shows that pre-match strength and form carry useful predictive information beyond league and season context. Its main limitation is that linear log-odds cannot automatically capture complex nonlinear relationships or interactions. Draws also remain intrinsically difficult to distinguish from narrow wins with the available predictors.

### 3.4.2 Linear Discriminant Analysis

Linear Discriminant Analysis (`MASS::lda`) was fitted as a classical linear baseline: it models each outcome class as multivariate-normal around its own mean, sharing one covariance matrix across classes, giving a different modelling assumption to the tree-based methods used elsewhere in the project. The context-only baseline used `competition_id` and `season_progress`; the refined model added the decorrelated pre-match differential features identified in Section 2.3.

Because LDA inverts a pooled covariance matrix across predictors, the near-duplicate features flagged in Section 2.3 were dropped, leaving `table_pos_diff`, `recent_goal_diff`, `venue_form_diff`, `h2h_diff`, `rest_days_diff`, `season_progress` and `competition_id` — re-selected independently inside every cross-validation fold so no later-season information leaks into the choice. Training-fold median imputation, missingness indicators and standardisation were applied before fitting, the same shared preprocessing design as the other models. The equal-covariance assumption was checked descriptively (within-class standard deviations and pairwise correlations are close across classes), offering partial support, though the features are not exactly multivariate-normal.

```{r}
#| label: lda-load-results
library(data.table)
library(knitr)
lda_res <- readRDS("outputs/member2_lda_results.rds")
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
```

As with the other models, predicting only the single most probable class rarely predicts a draw, so decision weights (home/draw/away, $\arg\max_k w_k \hat p_k$) were tuned on the five validation folds to maximise mean Macro-F1: the refined model's weights of 1 / 1.85 / 1.25 give a validation Macro-F1 of `r f3(lda_res$best_params$cv_macro_f1)`, against `r f3(lda_res$baseline_params$cv_macro_f1)` for the untuned context-only baseline.

**Final Test Results and Interpretation**

```{r}
#| label: lda-test-results
comparison <- as.data.table(lda_res$comparison)
test_table <- comparison[, .(
  Model = stage,
  Accuracy = f3(accuracy),
  `Macro-F1` = f3(macro_f1),
  `Recall: Home` = f3(recall_home_win),
  `Recall: Draw` = f3(recall_draw),
  `Recall: Away` = f3(recall_away_win)
)]
kable(test_table, caption = "Linear Discriminant Analysis results on the Final Test")
```

On the untouched Final Test set, the refined, weighted LDA reaches **Accuracy 0.483** and **Macro-F1 0.463**, against 0.201 for always predicting a home win. The most-probable-class rule alone gives a higher accuracy (0.510) but never predicts a draw, so the tuned weights trade some accuracy for a draw recall of 0.333 and the best overall Macro-F1. F1 by class: home win 0.585, draw 0.315, away win 0.489.

```{r}
#| label: lda-confusion-matrix
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Final refined LDA confusion matrix (tuned decision weights). Percentages show recall within each true outcome."
class_labels <- c(home_win = "Home win", draw = "Draw", away_win = "Away win")
cm_data <- as.data.table(as.data.frame(lda_res$test_metrics$confusion))
cm_data[, Share := Freq / sum(Freq), by = Truth]
cm_data[, Truth := factor(class_labels[as.character(Truth)], levels = class_labels)]
cm_data[, Predicted := factor(class_labels[as.character(Predicted)],
                              levels = rev(class_labels))]

ggplot(cm_data, aes(Truth, Predicted, fill = Share)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%d\n(%.0f%%)", Freq, 100 * Share)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f7fbff", high = "#2166ac", guide = "none") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  labs(x = "True result", y = "Predicted result")
```

`table_pos_diff` and `h2h_diff` carry the largest standardised LD1 discriminant weights, consistent with Random Forest's leading features (Section 3.4.5).

**Limitation.** As with every model tried, the draw class is hardest to separate: the engineered differentials capture relative team strength, not the closeness that produces a draw, and LDA's linear decision boundary is a further simplification on top of that.

### 3.4.4 Support Vector Machine

A support vector machine classifies by maximising the margin between classes, a different inductive bias from the probabilistic, linear, instance-based and ensemble methods above, which makes it a useful point of contrast. Two preprocessing steps were required that the tree-based models did not need: the RBF kernel is distance-based, so all numeric predictors were standardised, and `svm()` cannot accept missing values, so matchday-1 rows were median-imputed. Both were fitted inside each training fold.

```{r}
#| label: svm-load
library(data.table); library(knitr)
# Full fitting and tuning pipeline: Member4_SVM.qmd
svm_res <- readRDS("outputs/member4_svm_results.rds")
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
```

**Hyperparameter tuning.** Kernel choice was treated as a tuning decision rather than an assumption: a linear kernel was compared with an RBF kernel on the same five validation folds. Cost and gamma were then tuned by grid search. The first grid's optimum fell on its boundary, so the grid was extended until the optimum sat in the interior. Because kernel SVM training scales roughly quadratically with sample size, single-fit runtime was measured on 1,000, 2,000 and 4,000 rows before committing to a grid; the observed scaling confirmed the full grid was affordable on the largest fold of 18,159 matches.

```{r}
#| label: svm-tuning
cv  <- as.data.table(svm_res$cv_rbf)
lin <- as.data.table(svm_res$cv_linear)
kable(rbind(
  data.table(Kernel = "Linear", Cost = lin[which.max(cv_macro_f1)]$cost,
             Gamma = NA_real_,
             `Validation Macro-F1` = f3(max(lin$cv_macro_f1))),
  cv[order(-cv_macro_f1)][1:3, .(Kernel = "RBF", Cost = cost, Gamma = gamma,
             `Validation Macro-F1` = f3(cv_macro_f1))]),
  caption = "Best linear kernel and top three RBF configurations on the validation folds")
```

The RBF kernel was retained, consistent with the EDA finding that no single feature separates the three outcome classes linearly. The selected configuration was **cost 4, gamma 0.3**, with decision weights of 1 / `r svm_res$best_weights$w_draw` / `r svm_res$best_weights$w_away` tuned on the same folds.

```{r}
#| label: svm-test
cmp <- as.data.table(svm_res$comparison)
kable(cmp[!grepl("predict\\(\\)", stage),
          .(Stage = stage, Accuracy = f3(accuracy),
            `Balanced Accuracy` = f3(balanced_accuracy),
            `Macro-F1` = f3(macro_f1))],
      caption = "SVM performance on the Final Test")
```

Decision weighting raised Macro-F1 from 0.361 to 0.423 and draw recall from 0.085 to 0.218, at a cost of 3.6 percentage points of accuracy — the same trade-off observed for the other four models.

**Limitation.** Class probabilities from `e1071::svm` are obtained by Platt scaling fitted after training rather than directly from the model. This limited how much decision-weight tuning could improve minority-class recall relative to a probabilistic classifier such as LDA, and is the main reason the SVM finished behind the other four models on Macro-F1.

### 3.4.5 Random Forest

A Random Forest (`ranger`, 500 trees) averages many decision trees grown on bootstrap samples, each split choosing from a random subset of features. It is the only ensemble, non-parametric model in the comparison: it assumes no functional form and can capture interactions. Splits use one variable at a time, so no standardisation was needed, and all nine features were kept despite the correlated pairs in Section 2.3. Within each training fold, NAs were replaced by fold medians, with one 0/1 indicator per distinct missingness pattern so the forest can distinguish "no history yet" from "evenly matched". A probability forest was grown so that decision weights could be applied to its class probabilities.

```{r}
#| label: rf-load
library(data.table); library(knitr); library(ggplot2)
# Full fitting and tuning pipeline: Member5_Random_Forest.qmd
rf_res <- readRDS("outputs/member5_rf_results.rds")
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
rf_cv  <- as.data.table(rf_res$cv_table)
rf_bp  <- rf_res$best_params
rf_big <- rf_cv[min_node >= 50]          # leaves of at least 50 matches
```

**Hyperparameter tuning.** `mtry` (features tried per split) was searched over {1, 2, 3, 4, 6} and `min.node.size` (smallest leaf) over {10, 50, 100, 200, 400}, with decision weights tuned for each combination. The selected forest uses **mtry `r rf_bp$mtry`, min.node.size `r rf_bp$min_node`** and home/draw/away weights 1 / `r rf_bp$w_draw` / `r rf_bp$w_away`, giving a validation Macro-F1 of `r f3(rf_bp$cv_macro_f1)`. The surface was flat: all combinations with leaves of at least 50 matches scored `r f3(min(rf_big$cv_macro_f1))`–`r f3(max(rf_big$cv_macro_f1))`. Only very small leaves, which memorise individual results, did worse.

```{r}
#| label: rf-test
rf_cmp <- as.data.table(rf_res$comparison)[model == "Random Forest"]
kable(rf_cmp[, .(Stage = stage, Accuracy = f3(accuracy),
                 `Balanced Acc.` = f3(balanced_accuracy),
                 `Macro-F1` = f3(macro_f1), `Recall: Draw` = f3(recall_draw))],
      caption = "Random Forest performance on the Final Test")
```

```{r}
#| label: rf-test-values
rf_fin   <- rf_cmp[grepl("final", stage)]
rf_plain <- rf_cmp[grepl("most-probable", stage)]
rf_pc    <- rf_res$test_metrics$per_class
```

Weighting trades accuracy (`r f3(rf_plain$accuracy)` → `r f3(rf_fin$accuracy)`) for draw recall (`r f3(rf_plain$recall_draw)` → `r f3(rf_fin$recall_draw)`). Final class F1: home `r f3(rf_pc$f1[1])`, draw `r f3(rf_pc$f1[2])`, away `r f3(rf_pc$f1[3])`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rf-importance
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 2.3
#| fig-cap: "Random Forest permutation importance: the drop in out-of-bag accuracy when one feature is shuffled (training data only)."
imp <- as.data.table(rf_res$importance)
imp[, feature := as.character(feature)]
labels <- c(points_per_game_diff = "Season points per game",
            table_pos_diff = "League table position",
            recent_goal_diff = "Recent goal difference",
            h2h_diff = "Head-to-head record",
            form_points_diff = "Recent points (last 5)",
            venue_form_diff = "Home / away venue form",
            season_progress = "Season progress",
            rest_days_diff = "Rest days",
            competition_id = "League")
imp_plot <- rbind(imp[feature %in% names(labels), .(label = labels[feature], importance)],
                  data.table(label = "Missingness indicators (all)",
                             importance = imp[grepl("_na$", feature), sum(importance)]))
imp_plot[, label := factor(label, levels = label[order(importance)])]
ggplot(imp_plot, aes(100 * importance, label)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2166ac") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", 100 * importance)), hjust = -0.2, size = 2.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = "Accuracy lost when shuffled (percentage points)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```

Season-long strength dominates. Shuffling the points-per-game gap costs 3.4 percentage points of accuracy, twice any other feature, followed by table position and recent goal difference. League contributes nothing, consistent with the EDA.

**Limitation.** Permutation importance measures predictive reliance, not causal effect. It also splits credit between correlated features (`points_per_game_diff` and `table_pos_diff`, r = 0.90), understating the combined weight of season strength.

## 3.5 Hyperparameter Tuning

All five models were tuned on the same five expanding-window folds by mean validation Macro-F1, in two stages: model-specific hyperparameters, then draw and away-win decision weights on the class probabilities ($\arg\max_k w_k \hat p_k$, home weight 1). The Final Test played no part in tuning.

```{r}
#| label: tuning-summary
library(data.table); library(knitr)
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
mlr_t <- readRDS("outputs/member1_mlr_results.rds")
lda_t <- readRDS("outputs/member2_lda_results.rds")
knn_t <- readRDS("outputs/member3_knn_results.rds")
svm_t <- readRDS("outputs/member4_svm_results.rds")
rf_t  <- readRDS("outputs/member5_rf_results.rds")

mlr_cv  <- as.data.table(mlr_t$cv_table)[order(-cv_macro_f1)][1]
lda_cv  <- as.data.table(lda_t$cv_table)
lda_pl  <- lda_cv[w_draw == 1 & w_away == 1]$cv_macro_f1
kb <- knn_t$best_params; sb <- svm_t$best; sw <- svm_t$best_weights; rb <- rf_t$best_params

tune_tab <- data.table(
  Model = c("Multinomial logistic regression", "LDA", "kNN", "SVM (RBF)", "Random Forest"),
  `Hyperparameters searched` = c(
    "Feature set; decay {0, 10⁻⁴, …, 1}",
    "None (redundant features dropped per fold)",
    "k {5, …, 501}; league weight {0.3, 1}; no-history flag",
    "Kernel; cost {1, 4, 16}; gamma {0.15, 0.3, 0.6}",
    "mtry {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}; min.node.size {10, …, 400}"),
  Selected = c(
    sprintf("No venue form; decay %g", mlr_t$best_decay),
    "—",
    sprintf("k = %d; weight %g; flag on", kb$k, kb$lw),
    sprintf("cost %g; gamma %g", sb$cost, sb$gamma),
    sprintf("mtry %d; min.node %d", rb$mtry, rb$min_node)),
  `Weights (draw / away)` = c(
    sprintf("%.2f / %.2f", mlr_t$decision_weights[["draw"]], mlr_t$decision_weights[["away_win"]]),
    sprintf("%.2f / %.2f", lda_t$best_params$w_draw, lda_t$best_params$w_away),
    sprintf("%.2f / %.2f", kb$w_draw, kb$w_away),
    sprintf("%.2f / %.2f", sw$w_draw, sw$w_away),
    sprintf("%.2f / %.2f", rb$w_draw, rb$w_away)),
  `Val. Macro-F1: unweighted → weighted` = c(
    paste(f3(mlr_cv$cv_macro_f1_plain), "→", f3(mlr_cv$cv_macro_f1)),
    paste(f3(lda_pl), "→", f3(lda_t$best_params$cv_macro_f1)),
    paste(f3(kb$cv_macro_f1_plain), "→", f3(kb$cv_macro_f1)),
    paste(f3(sb$cv_macro_f1), "→", f3(sw$cv_macro_f1)),
    paste(f3(rb$cv_macro_f1_plain), "→", f3(rb$cv_macro_f1))))
kable(tune_tab, caption = "Tuning choices and validation Macro-F1 for the five refined models")
```

- **Hyperparameters mattered little.** Surfaces were flat: MLR decay from 0 to 1 changes validation Macro-F1 by under 0.001, and Random Forest varies by about 0.004 once leaves hold 50+ matches. Where settings mattered, smoother options won (very large k, large leaves), as expected for a weak, noisy signal.
- **Decision weights mattered most.** Unweighted, the models rarely predict draws (validation Macro-F1 0.37–0.40). The weights add 0.03–0.09, and all five converged on similar values (draw 1.70–2.00, away 1.25–1.50), which points to a shared problem: a draw is seldom the most probable outcome.
- **Grid boundaries.** The SVM grid was extended until its optimum was interior. The kNN optimum (k = `r kb$k`) lies on its grid's upper edge, so a larger k might help slightly. The grid was not extended after the test results were seen.

Choosing settings and weights on the same folds makes validation scores mildly optimistic; Section 4 reports the unbiased test results.

# 4. Model Evaluation and Selection

## 4.1 Evaluation Metrics

Four metrics are reported for every model, computed by a single shared scoring function on the same 5,256-match Final Test so that differences reflect model behaviour rather than differences in measurement.
Macro-F1 is the primary metric and determines the final model choice. Accuracy alone is unsuitable for this problem: always predicting a home win achieves 43.0% accuracy while scoring zero on two of the three outcomes. Macro-F1 averages the F1 score across all three classes equally, so a model that abandons draws — the minority class at 25% of matches — is penalised rather than rewarded. This was decided before any model was fitted.
Accuracy is reported as a supporting measure because it is the most intuitive summary and allows direct comparison against the majority-class reference of 0.430.
Balanced accuracy, the mean of the three class recalls, provides a second imbalance-robust view and is unaffected by how often each class is predicted.
Class-level precision, recall and F1 are reported for home wins, draws and away wins separately, since the aggregate metrics conceal which outcomes a model handles well. Draw recall in particular proved decisive: before decision weighting, several models identified almost no draws despite achieving reasonable accuracy.
Confusion matrices are used diagnostically to show not only how often a model is wrong but in which direction, which Section 4.3 draws on when comparing the final candidates.

## 4.2 Model Performance Comparison

```{r}
#| label: final-comparison
library(data.table); library(knitr)

rows <- rbindlist(lapply(
  list.files("outputs", pattern = "member._.*comparison_row\\.csv$",
             full.names = TRUE), fread), fill = TRUE)
final <- rows[grepl("final", stage, ignore.case = TRUE)][order(-macro_f1)]

kable(final[, .(Model = model,
                Accuracy = sprintf("%.3f", accuracy),
                `Balanced Acc.` = sprintf("%.3f", balanced_accuracy),
                `Macro-F1` = sprintf("%.3f", macro_f1),
                `Recall: Draw` = sprintf("%.3f", recall_draw))],
      caption = "Final test-set performance of all five models (5,256 matches)")
```

LDA achieved the highest Macro-F1 at 0.463, followed by multinomial logistic regression (0.457), kNN (0.453) and random forest (0.451), with the SVM behind at 0.423. The ranking is metric-dependent: kNN was the most accurate model (0.486) but third on Macro-F1, while LDA was third on accuracy. Every model exceeded the majority-class Macro-F1 of 0.201 by a wide margin while improving accuracy by only four to six percentage points, showing that the gain is concentrated in the minority classes rather than in overall correctness. Draw recall ranges from 0.218 to 0.375 across the five models, confirming that draws remain the limiting class for all of them regardless of method.

## 4.3 Final Model Selection

The four leading models differ by only 0.012 in Macro-F1 across 5,256 matches, a margin too small to attribute confidently to genuine differences in model quality. These four are therefore treated as equivalent on predictive performance; only the SVM can be separated on results alone, and the reason for its weaker showing is documented in Section 3.4.4.
LDA is selected as the final model. Where predictive performance is equivalent, selection must rest on other grounds, and LDA is the strongest on each. It is the most interpretable of the candidates, since each predictor enters through a single discriminant coefficient whose sign and magnitude can be read directly. It is the cheapest to train, with no hyperparameters requiring a search. And it estimates class probabilities directly from the model rather than deriving them afterwards, which made decision-weight tuning more effective for it than for the SVM, where Platt-scaled probabilities limited the achievable gain. Claiming a clear winner on a 0.006 margin would overstate what the evidence supports; choosing the simplest model among equals is the defensible conclusion.
Class-level performance supports this reading. LDA recovers 33% of draws with 30% precision, while identifying 58% of home wins and 47% of away wins. No model in the comparison handles draws well, and the pattern is consistent across all five despite their differing assumptions, which points to the feature set rather than the choice of algorithm as the binding constraint.

## 4.4 Process Reflection

The Data Investigation Process shaped this project most visibly at the exploration stage. Two forms of target leakage were identified before any model was fitted: the supplied league position columns record standings after each match, and the club attribute fields are a single present-day snapshot rather than values contemporaneous with each fixture. Had modelling begun directly from the raw data, the project would have reported substantially inflated results built on information unavailable before kick-off. The sequencing of the process — explore, then engineer, then model — is what surfaced both.
Fixing the shared infrastructure before any modelling began proved equally important. Agreeing the chronological split, the validation folds and a single scoring function in advance meant that five models, fitted independently by five people, could be compared without re-running anything or reconciling differing definitions.
Two things would be done differently. Feature engineering was assigned as a blocking deliverable but was not completed on schedule and was eventually built by another member, which delayed every downstream model; a task that the whole team depends on needs a firm date and a named backup. Second, decision-weight tuning was adopted by individual members before the group agreed on it, briefly making the results non-comparable until it was applied uniformly. A refinement that changes the ranking on the primary metric should be a group decision made at the planning stage rather than an individual one discovered during comparison.

# 5. Conclusion and Insights

```{r}
#| label: conclusion-values
library(data.table)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
f3  <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
all_rows <- rbindlist(lapply(
  list.files("outputs", pattern = "member._.*comparison_row\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE),
  fread), fill = TRUE)
fin  <- all_rows[grepl("final", stage, ignore.case = TRUE)][order(-macro_f1)]
best <- fin[1]
maj  <- all_rows[model == "Majority class"][1]
ctx  <- all_rows[grepl("^Baseline", stage)]          # league + season progress only

# Random Forest test-set probabilities by season points-per-game gap
rf_c <- readRDS("outputs/member5_rf_results.rds")
tp   <- merge(as.data.table(rf_c$test_predictions),
              as.data.table(readRDS("data/model_data.rds"))[, .(game_id, points_per_game_diff)],
              by = "game_id")
even <- tp[points_per_game_diff > -0.25 & points_per_game_diff <= 0.25]
fav  <- tp[points_per_game_diff > 1.25]
```

## 5.1 Answer to the Research Question

Pre-match characteristics classify match outcomes **partially**: clearly better than simple rules, but far from reliably. The selected model, `r best$model`, classifies `r pct(best$accuracy)` of 2023/24–2025/26 matches correctly with Macro-F1 `r f3(best$macro_f1)`. Always predicting a home win gives `r pct(maj$accuracy)` and `r f3(maj$macro_f1)`, and no model using only league and season progress exceeds `r f3(max(ctx$macro_f1))`. All five refined models fall within `r f3(min(fin$macro_f1))`–`r f3(max(fin$macro_f1))`, so the conclusion does not depend on the method. Predictability is uneven across outcomes. Home and away wins are separated moderately well (`r best$model` F1 `r f3(best$f1_home_win)` and `r f3(best$f1_away_win)`), but draws are not (draw F1 `r f3(min(fin$f1_draw))`–`r f3(max(fin$f1_draw))` across models). Pre-match information explains part of a result; much of it remains unpredictable before kick-off.

## 5.2 Key Insights

1. **Season-long strength carries most of the signal.** Season points per game and table position lead the Random Forest importance, and table position has one of LDA's two largest discriminant weights. Five-match form adds less, and league adds nothing. A season-to-date average is a steadier measure of quality than a short, noisy run of results.
2. **The decision rule mattered more than the algorithm.** Re-weighting raised each model's test Macro-F1 by 0.03–0.08 (Random Forest: 0.383 to 0.451), while the four leading algorithms differ by only `r f3(fin$macro_f1[1] - fin$macro_f1[4])`.
3. **Draws are hard for a structural reason.** For evenly matched teams (points-per-game gap within ±0.25), the forest's average draw probability is `r pct(mean(even$draw))`, close to the observed `r pct(mean(even$truth == "draw"))`. A home win is still more likely (`r pct(mean(even$home_win))` predicted, `r pct(mean(even$truth == "home_win"))` observed). A draw is almost never the most likely outcome, so predicting draws costs 2–5 percentage points of accuracy.
4. **The outputs are most useful as probabilities.** Predicted probabilities track observed frequencies. When the home side leads by more than 1.25 points per game, the forest predicts a `r pct(mean(fav$home_win))` home-win chance against `r pct(mean(fav$truth == "home_win"))` observed. For analysts and media, the models give dependable likelihoods for clear favourites but little separation in close match-ups.

## 5.3 Limitations and Future Improvements

**Data.** Club attributes are a single present-day snapshot and were excluded, so the models have no time-accurate measure of squad quality, injuries or transfers. Early-season matches have little history and were median-imputed, so predictions near matchday 1 are close to average. The training period also includes the 2020 no-crowd seasons, when home advantage temporarily fell.

**Modelling.** The features measure the *difference* between teams, not how *even* a match is, which is the main reason draws remain hard. No formal significance test was run, so the small gaps between the top four models are treated as ties rather than a ranking.

**Future improvements.**

- Add evenness features from the existing data, such as the absolute strength gap and each team's recent draw rate, and test whether draw F1 improves.
- Replace snapshot attributes with a time-varying rating, such as an Elo-style rating updated from past results only.
- Fit an ordinal model (away win < draw < home win), which places the draw explicitly between the two wins, and compare models with a paired test such as McNemar's test.
